newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM urges "Big Bang" markets reform by 2001.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM urges "Big Bang" markets reform by 2001.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called on Monday for the rapid reform of the nation's financial markets in a Tokyo-style "Big Bang" to be completed by the year 2001.

After meeting the prime minister, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters his ministry would aim to implement steps to make Japan's financial markets freer, fairer and more global by the target date.
"This is going to be Tokyo's 'Big Bang'," Mitsuzuka said, referring to British financial reforms in 1986 that removed various barriers in the financial industry.
Hashimoto unveiled his financial deregulation plan at a meeting with Mitsuzuka and Justice Minister Isao Matsuura, who said his ministry would cooperate fully in enacting the reforms.

Hashimoto formed a new cabinet last Thursday made up solely of Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lawmakers, the first time the conservative, pro-business party has ruled on its own since being booted out of power in 1993.

"While proceeding with the disposal of problem loans, Japan aims at rejuvenating its financial markets as an international market equivalent to those in New York and London by 2001," Hashimoto said in a statement.

Some pundits have wondered how serious Hashimoto and the LDP are about drastic deregulation, although others say the politically astute prime minister is well aware of the need to open Japanese markets to competition to ensure the economy flourishes in the 21st century.
The following are the main points of the financial reform plans, most of which are already being discussed by government advisory councils.
For the creation of freer markets:
-- Banks, securities houses and insurance firms should be allowed to enter each others' business areas.
-- Banks and other financial institutions should be allowed to deal in more products in a bid to meet investors' wide range of needs.
-- Japan will look into the liberalisation of financial market commission fees.
-- Participation in foreign exchange transactions, currently limited to banks authorised by the government, should be liberalised.
-- Considering the effective use of individual savings, which now total 1,200 trillion yen ($10.81 trillion).
To create fairer markets;

-- Financial institutions should be required to make satisfactory disclosure of information to investors and depositors and clarify relevant rules so as to make market participants responsible for their investment.
-- Market participants will be more severely punished if they violate the rules regarding their involvement in the markets.
To create more internationalised markets;
-- Investment in financial derivatives should be promoted in Japan by revising Japan's accounting system and relevant laws to meet global standards.
-- A supervisory system on a global scale should be established. The Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations are working on setting up up such a system.
